front: What is the DAG-based video transcoding architecture, and what are the six main components?
back: The architecture uses a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) to model transcoding tasks: 1) Preprocessor — splits video into GOPs, generates the DAG from config files, caches segments for retry. 2) DAG Scheduler — splits the DAG into stages and enqueues tasks. 3) Resource Manager — has a task queue, worker queue, and running queue; its scheduler optimally assigns tasks to workers. 4) Task Workers — execute encoding, thumbnail generation, watermarking, etc. 5) Temporary Storage — caches metadata in memory, video/audio in blob storage. 6) Encoded Video — the final output in multiple formats/resolutions.

graph TD
    Video --> Preprocessor
    Preprocessor -->|DAG| DAGScheduler[DAG Scheduler]
    DAGScheduler --> ResourceManager[Resource Manager]
    ResourceManager --> TaskWorkers[Task Workers]
    TaskWorkers --> TempStorage[Temporary Storage]
    TaskWorkers --> EncodedVideo[Encoded Video Output]

front: What are the three speed optimizations for YouTube's video upload pipeline?
back: 1) Parallelize video uploading: Split the video into smaller chunks (GOP alignment) on the client side. This enables fast resumable uploads — if a chunk fails, only that chunk is retried. 2) Upload centers close to users: Use geographically distributed CDN endpoints as upload centers (US users upload to North America, China to Asia). 3) Parallelism via message queues: Introduce message queues between pipeline stages so encoding doesn't wait for download to finish — modules process events independently, enabling pipeline parallelism.

front: What is a pre-signed upload URL, and why does YouTube's design use it instead of letting clients upload directly to storage?
back: A pre-signed URL is a time-limited, permission-scoped URL generated by API servers that grants upload access to a specific storage location. Flow: client requests a pre-signed URL from the API → API generates it → client uploads directly to storage using that URL. This ensures only authenticated, authorized users can upload to the correct location. Without it, clients would need storage credentials directly, creating a massive security vulnerability. AWS calls it 'pre-signed URL'; Azure calls it 'Shared Access Signature'.

front: What are four strategies to reduce CDN costs for a video streaming platform, and what principle underlies all of them?
back: 1) Serve only the most popular videos from CDN; less popular ones stream from origin storage. 2) For unpopular content, encode fewer versions and transcode on-demand. 3) Regional CDN distribution — don't replicate regionally popular videos globally. 4) Build your own CDN by partnering with ISPs (like Netflix's Open Connect). The underlying principle: content popularity follows a long-tail distribution, so optimize aggressively for the popular head while accepting higher latency for the long tail.

front: What are the key differences between designing for live streaming vs. video-on-demand (VOD), and why can't you simply reuse the YouTube VOD architecture?
back: Live streaming differs in three critical ways: 1) Latency requirements are much stricter — viewers expect near-real-time, so you may need different streaming protocols (e.g., WebRTC over HLS). 2) Parallelism is reduced — data arrives in small real-time chunks that are already sequentially processed, unlike VOD where an entire file can be split and encoded in parallel. 3) Error handling must be faster — any retry or recovery that takes too long means lost live content. You can't re-encode a frame that's already passed.

front: What are the three safety mechanisms for protecting copyrighted video content on YouTube?
back: 1) Digital Rights Management (DRM): Platform-specific encryption — Apple FairPlay, Google Widevine, Microsoft PlayReady. The player decrypts content at playback using authorized licenses. 2) AES encryption with authorization policies: Encrypt the video stream; only users with valid authorization tokens can decrypt and view. 3) Visual watermarking: Overlay identifying information on the video to deter redistribution and enable tracing of leaked content back to the source.

front: Why is the Resource Manager in the transcoding pipeline critical, and how does its task scheduler work?
back: The Resource Manager has three queues: task queue (priority-ordered pending tasks), worker queue (worker utilization info), and running queue (active task-worker bindings). The scheduler: (1) picks the highest-priority task, (2) selects the optimal worker based on capacity, (3) binds the task to the worker and tracks it in the running queue, (4) removes the binding when complete. This prevents hot workers from being overloaded while idle ones sit unused — essential when transcoding millions of videos with varying complexity.

front: Interview tip: In a YouTube design interview, what two high-level flows should you propose immediately, and why?
back: Propose the video uploading flow and the video streaming flow as two separate subsystems. This shows the interviewer you understand the fundamental asymmetry: uploading is write-heavy, compute-intensive (transcoding), and latency-tolerant; streaming is read-heavy, bandwidth-intensive, and latency-sensitive (CDN-served). The interviewer will then let you pick which to deep-dive. Choose based on your strengths — uploading showcases distributed systems (DAG pipelines, queues), streaming showcases CDN/caching architecture.

front: For Google Drive with 50M users and 10M DAU, what are the key capacity estimates and what do they tell you about the design?
back: Total storage: 50M users × 10GB free = 500 Petabytes. Upload QPS: 10M × 2 uploads/day / 86400 ≈ 240 QPS (peak 480). The storage number (500PB) screams 'you need cloud object storage like S3' — no self-managed storage is practical. The low QPS (240) means the bottleneck isn't request throughput but rather bandwidth (500KB × 240 = 120MB/s sustained upload), storage cost, and sync consistency. This shifts the design focus toward efficient sync, deduplication, and storage tiering.

front: What is the role of block servers in Google Drive's upload architecture, and what three operations do they perform on each file?
back: Block servers handle the heavy lifting of file uploads. For each file they: 1) Split the file into smaller blocks (max 4MB each, per Dropbox's approach). 2) Compress each block using appropriate algorithms (gzip/bzip2 for text, different algorithms for images/video). 3) Encrypt each block before uploading to cloud storage. Only modified blocks are transferred on updates (delta sync), dramatically reducing bandwidth. Each block gets a unique hash stored in the metadata DB, enabling deduplication and file reconstruction by joining blocks in order.

front: How does Google Drive handle sync conflicts when two users modify the same file simultaneously?
back: The system uses a first-writer-wins strategy: the first version processed by the system succeeds, and the later version receives a conflict. When User 2 gets a conflict, the system presents both copies — User 2's local version and the latest server version — and User 2 must manually merge them or choose one to keep. For real-time collaborative editing (Google Docs), more sophisticated algorithms like Differential Synchronization or OT (Operational Transformation) are needed, but those are explicitly out of scope.

front: Why does Google Drive use long polling instead of WebSocket for its notification service?
back: Google Drive's notification pattern is fundamentally different from chat: file changes are infrequent with no burst of data. WebSocket's persistent bidirectional connection would be overkill — most of the time there's nothing to send. Long polling is more efficient here: each client holds a long-lived connection to the notification service; when a file change is detected, the connection closes (signaling the client to fetch updates from the metadata server). The client then immediately opens a new long poll connection.

front: What three techniques does Google Drive use to reduce storage costs while maintaining file version history?
back: 1) De-duplicate data blocks: Two blocks with the same hash value are stored only once, eliminating redundancy at the account level. 2) Intelligent backup strategy: Set a limit on versions stored (oldest replaced) and keep only 'valuable' versions — e.g., for frequently edited files, don't save every single keystroke-level revision. 3) Move infrequently accessed data to cold storage (e.g., Amazon S3 Glacier): data older than a certain threshold is automatically archived to cheaper storage tiers.

front: Why does the design route uploads through block servers instead of uploading directly from client to cloud storage? What is the tradeoff?
back: Going through block servers centralizes chunking, compression, and encryption logic on the server side. Direct upload is faster (one transfer instead of two), but has serious drawbacks: (1) the same chunking/compression/encryption logic must be reimplemented on every platform (iOS, Android, Web) — error-prone and costly. (2) Client-side encryption is less secure because clients can be hacked or manipulated. The block server approach trades upload latency for security, consistency, and engineering simplicity.

front: The metadata layer requires strong consistency. Why is a relational database chosen over NoSQL, and what cache invalidation strategy is used?
back: Strong consistency is non-negotiable — a file cannot appear differently to different clients simultaneously. Relational databases natively support ACID properties (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability), making strong consistency straightforward. NoSQL databases default to eventual consistency, and programming ACID-like guarantees into the application's sync logic is complex and error-prone. For the metadata cache: invalidate on every database write to ensure cache and DB always agree. This write-invalidate pattern sacrifices some cache hit rate but guarantees consistency.

front: Describe the download flow when a file is modified by another user. How does Client 2 learn about and retrieve the changes?
back: 1) Notification service informs Client 2 that a file changed (via long polling connection close). 2) Client 2 requests updated metadata from API servers. 3) API servers query metadata DB for change details. 4) Metadata returned to Client 2 (which blocks changed, new hashes). 5) Client 2 requests only the changed blocks from block servers. 6) Block servers fetch those blocks from cloud storage. 7) Client 2 reconstructs the file from existing local blocks + new downloaded blocks. Only delta blocks transfer — not the whole file.

front: What is the database schema design for Google Drive, and how does the Block table enable file versioning and reconstruction?
back: Five core tables: User (username, email, profile), Device (device info, push_id for notifications — a user can have multiple), Namespace (root directory per user), File (latest file metadata), File_Version (version history, rows are read-only to preserve integrity), Block (block hash, size, order, linked to file version). front: How do hash maps achieve O(1) average lookup time?
back: Hash maps apply a hash function to keys, mapping them to array indices for direct access. The hash function distributes keys uniformly across buckets, so finding a value requires computing the hash and indexing into the array — both constant-time operations. Average case is O(1), but worst case degrades to O(n) if all keys collide into one bucket.

front: How do hash maps handle collisions, and what are the two main strategies?
back: Chaining stores colliding entries in a linked list (or tree) at each bucket — simple but uses extra memory. Open addressing probes for the next empty slot using linear probing, quadratic probing, or double hashing — better cache locality but degrades as load factor rises. Most production implementations (Java HashMap, Python dict) use a hybrid approach.

front: What is a B-tree, and why is it the default index structure in relational databases?
back: A B-tree is a self-balancing tree where each node holds multiple keys and has multiple children, keeping the tree wide and shallow. This minimizes disk I/O because each node read fetches many keys in one page-sized block. All leaves are at the same depth, guaranteeing O(log n) for search, insert, and delete. PostgreSQL, MySQL InnoDB, and SQLite all use B-tree variants for indexes.

front: How do LSM trees work, and why are they write-optimized compared to B-trees?
back: LSM trees buffer writes in an in-memory sorted structure (memtable). When full, it's flushed to disk as an immutable sorted file (SSTable). Background compaction merges SSTables to reclaim space and maintain read performance. Writes are sequential (append-only), making them 10-100x faster than B-tree random writes. Used in LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra, and HBase.

front: LSM trees vs B-trees: when would you choose each?
back: LSM trees excel at write-heavy workloads (logging, time-series, event stores) because writes are sequential and buffered. B-trees are better for read-heavy workloads with frequent point lookups because data is in-place and doesn't require checking multiple levels. LSM trees suffer from write amplification during compaction; B-trees suffer from write amplification on random inserts that split pages.

front: What is a skip list, and why does Redis use it for sorted sets?
back: A skip list is a layered linked list where higher layers skip over multiple elements, enabling O(log n) search by starting at the top and dropping down. It provides the same time complexity as balanced BSTs but is simpler to implement and supports concurrent access more easily. Redis uses skip lists for sorted sets because they allow efficient range queries and O(log n) insertion without the complexity of red-black trees.

front: What is a Bloom filter, and why does it allow false positives but not false negatives?
back: A Bloom filter is a bit array with k hash functions. To add an element, hash it k times and set those bits to 1. To check membership, verify all k bits are set. False positives occur because different elements can set overlapping bits. False negatives are impossible because if the element was added, its bits are guaranteed to be 1. Used in Cassandra, BigTable, and Chrome's safe browsing to avoid expensive disk/network lookups.

  E --> H2["Hash2 → bit 7"]
  E --> H3["Hash3 → bit 11"]
  H1 --> BA["Bit Array:\n0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0 1 0 0 0"]
  Q["Query Y"] --> C{"All bits set?"}

front: What is a Merkle tree, and how is it used for data verification in distributed systems?
back: A Merkle tree is a binary tree where each leaf is a hash of a data block, and each internal node is a hash of its children. To verify any single block, you only need the hashes along the path to the root — O(log n) hashes instead of the full dataset. Used in Git for content addressing, blockchain for transaction verification, and Cassandra/DynamoDB for anti-entropy repair between replicas.

front: What is a trie (prefix tree), and what are its main applications?
back: A trie stores strings character by character along tree edges, so shared prefixes share nodes. Lookup time is O(m) where m is the key length, independent of the number of stored keys. Primary uses: autocomplete (find all words starting with a prefix), IP routing tables (longest prefix match), and spell checkers. Space-optimized variants like radix tries compress single-child chains into one node.

front: Hash map vs trie vs B-tree: how do their lookup characteristics differ?
back: Hash maps give O(1) average lookup for exact keys but can't do range queries or prefix searches. Tries give O(m) lookup (m = key length) and excel at prefix queries but use more memory. B-trees give O(log n) lookup and support both range queries and ordered iteration, making them ideal for databases. Choose based on access pattern: exact match → hash map, prefix → trie, range → B-tree.

front: What is consistent hashing, and which data structure makes it efficient?
back: Consistent hashing maps both servers and keys onto a ring (0 to 2^32). Each key is assigned to the first server clockwise on the ring. When a server is added or removed, only keys in the affected segment move — O(K/N) keys instead of O(K). The ring is typically backed by a sorted map (balanced BST or skip list) for O(log N) lookups. Virtual nodes improve balance.

front: What is a count-min sketch, and how does it differ from a Bloom filter?
back: A count-min sketch estimates frequency counts using a 2D array of counters with multiple hash functions. Each element increments k counters; querying returns the minimum across k positions. While Bloom filters answer 'is it present?', count-min sketches answer 'how many times?' — both are probabilistic and can overcount but never undercount. Used in network traffic analysis and trending detection.

front: What is HyperLogLog, and why is it used for counting unique items at scale?
back: HyperLogLog estimates cardinality (count of distinct elements) using only ~12KB of memory regardless of dataset size. It works by hashing elements and observing the distribution of leading zeros — more leading zeros implies more unique items. Accuracy is ~0.81% with the standard 16K registers. Redis uses it via PFADD/PFCOUNT for unique visitor counting.

front: Bloom filter vs count-min sketch vs HyperLogLog: what question does each answer?
back: Bloom filter: 'Is this element in the set?' (set membership). Count-min sketch: 'How often has this element appeared?' (frequency estimation). HyperLogLog: 'How many distinct elements exist?' (cardinality estimation). All three are probabilistic, use sublinear space, and trade exact accuracy for massive memory savings at scale.

front: What is a write-ahead log (WAL), and why is it critical for database reliability?
back: A WAL records every change to an append-only log file before applying it to the actual data pages. If the system crashes mid-write, the database replays the WAL to recover committed transactions. This converts random writes into sequential appends (faster on disk) and provides durability guarantees. Used in PostgreSQL, SQLite, etcd, and Kafka.

front: What happens when the load balancer fails, and how do systems mitigate this?
back: A single load balancer is a single point of failure — if it dies, all traffic to the cluster stops. Mitigation: deploy active-passive LB pairs with a floating VIP (virtual IP) that fails over via keepalived/VRRP in seconds. Cloud LBs (ALB, NLB) are inherently distributed across AZs. DNS-based failover can also redirect to a standby LB, though DNS TTLs add delay.

front: What is the thundering herd problem when cache goes down?
back: When a cache node fails or a popular key expires, all concurrent requests miss the cache simultaneously and hit the database. This can overwhelm the DB with N identical queries at once. Mitigations: cache stampede locks (only one request rebuilds, others wait), staggered TTLs with jitter, request coalescing (singleflight pattern), and cache warming before expiry.

front: What happens when the master DB fails, and what are the failover tradeoffs?
back: Writes stop immediately. Automated failover promotes a replica to master, but risks data loss if the replica was behind (asynchronous replication). Synchronous replication avoids data loss but adds write latency. Semi-synchronous (MySQL) or quorum-based (CockroachDB) are middle grounds. Failover takes seconds to minutes; applications need retry logic and connection pool refresh.

front: What happens when a message queue consumer dies mid-processing?
back: If the consumer crashes before acknowledging, the message remains unacked and the broker redelivers it after a visibility timeout (SQS) or nack/timeout (RabbitMQ). This means consumers MUST be idempotent — the same message may be processed more than once. If the consumer acks before completing work, the message is lost. Dead letter queues capture messages that repeatedly fail processing.

front: What is the split-brain problem during a network partition?
back: When a network partition separates nodes that can't communicate, both sides may believe they are the active leader and accept writes independently. This leads to conflicting data that's hard to reconcile when the partition heals. Solutions: quorum-based leader election (majority required), fencing tokens (old leader's writes rejected), or choosing CP over AP per the CAP theorem.

front: How do cascading failures propagate, and how do you prevent them?
back: Service A fails → Service B's requests to A time out, exhausting B's thread pool → B becomes slow → Services calling B also back up → system-wide failure. Prevention: circuit breakers stop calling failing services, bulkheads isolate resource pools per dependency, timeouts prevent thread exhaustion, and load shedding drops excess requests early. Each layer must fail independently.

front: What is the difference between graceful degradation and hard failure?
back: Graceful degradation: the system continues working with reduced functionality (e.g., serving cached results when the DB is down, disabling recommendations but keeping core search). Hard failure: the entire system stops when any critical component fails. Graceful degradation requires explicit design — feature flags, fallback paths, and priority tiers for which features to shed first.

front: How does the circuit breaker pattern work, and what are its three states?
back: A circuit breaker wraps calls to an external service and tracks failures. Closed (normal): requests pass through; if failures exceed a threshold, trip to Open. Open: requests fail immediately without calling the service, preventing cascade. After a timeout, transition to Half-Open. Half-Open: allow one probe request through; if it succeeds, return to Closed, otherwise back to Open.

stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> Closed
  Closed --> Open : Failure threshold exceeded
  Open --> HalfOpen : Timeout expires
  HalfOpen --> Closed : Probe succeeds
  HalfOpen --> Open : Probe fails
  Closed --> Closed : Success / below threshold

front: Why do retries need exponential backoff with jitter?
back: Simple retries at fixed intervals cause synchronized retry storms — all clients retry at the same time, overwhelming the recovering service. Exponential backoff spaces retries further apart (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s...). Adding random jitter (±0-100% of the interval) desynchronizes clients so retries spread over time instead of arriving in waves. Cap the maximum delay and set a retry limit.

front: What is a dead letter queue (DLQ), and when are messages sent there?
back: A DLQ is a separate queue that receives messages that repeatedly fail processing — typically after exceeding a maximum retry count. This prevents poison messages from blocking the main queue forever. DLQs enable manual inspection, alerting, and replaying once the bug is fixed. SQS, RabbitMQ, and Kafka all support DLQ configuration. Always monitor DLQ depth as a signal of processing errors.

front: What is the difference between active and passive health checks?
back: Active health checks: the load balancer or orchestrator periodically sends probe requests (HTTP GET /health, TCP connect) to each instance and removes unhealthy ones from the pool. Passive health checks: the system monitors real traffic responses — if an instance returns errors or times out on actual requests, it's marked unhealthy. Best practice: use both. Active detects down instances; passive catches degraded ones.

front: How does blue-green deployment achieve zero-downtime releases?
back: Two identical production environments exist: Blue (current live) and Green (new version). Deploy and test the new version on Green while Blue serves traffic. Once verified, switch the load balancer/DNS to point to Green. If issues arise, instantly roll back by switching back to Blue. Cost: double infrastructure during deployment. Requires stateless apps or shared database with backward-compatible migrations.

front: How does canary deployment reduce release risk?
back: Route a small percentage of traffic (e.g., 5%) to the new version while 95% stays on the old. Monitor error rates, latency, and business metrics on the canary. If healthy, gradually increase traffic (5% → 25% → 50% → 100%). If the canary shows problems, roll back only the 5% — most users never see the issue. More granular than blue-green but requires traffic splitting infrastructure.

front: What are feature flags, and how do they decouple deployment from release?
back: Feature flags are conditional checks in code that enable or disable functionality at runtime without redeploying. This lets you deploy code to production with the feature off, then enable it for specific users, percentage rollouts, or all at once. If the feature causes issues, toggle it off instantly. Enables trunk-based development and A/B testing. Tools: LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or simple config/DB flags.

front: What is chaos engineering, and what does it prove that testing cannot?
back: Chaos engineering deliberately injects failures in production (kill instances, add latency, drop packets) to verify the system actually recovers as designed. Unit and integration tests prove code logic; chaos tests prove the system's resilience under real conditions — failover actually works, alerts fire, runbooks are correct. Netflix's Chaos Monkey randomly kills instances; Gremlin and Litmus provide structured chaos experiments.

front: What are Redis's key performance characteristics?
back: Redis handles ~100K-200K ops/s on a single thread using an event loop and in-memory data structures. It is single-threaded for commands (avoiding lock contention), stores everything in RAM for sub-millisecond latency, and supports data structures beyond simple KV (lists, sets, sorted sets, streams). Memory is the bottleneck — typically 25-100GB per instance.

front: What throughput can Kafka achieve, and what enables it?
back: Kafka can handle ~1M messages/s per partition by using append-only sequential writes, zero-copy transfer from disk to network, batched I/O, and page cache. Throughput scales linearly with partitions across brokers. Retention is time or size-based (not consumption-based), so multiple consumers read the same log independently. Typical end-to-end latency is 2-10ms.

front: What is PostgreSQL's typical throughput, and when does it hit limits?
back: PostgreSQL handles ~5K-10K simple queries/s on a single node with proper indexing. It provides full ACID transactions, complex joins, and strong consistency. Vertical scaling (more CPU/RAM) helps to a point, but write-heavy workloads hit limits around 10-20K TPS due to MVCC overhead and WAL writes. Read replicas scale reads; sharding (Citus) scales writes.

front: What makes DynamoDB's performance model different from traditional databases?
back: DynamoDB provides single-digit millisecond latency at any scale by distributing data across partitions automatically. You provision read/write capacity units (or use on-demand mode), and throughput scales horizontally without operational overhead. Tradeoff: limited query patterns (partition key + sort key only), eventual consistency by default, and 400KB item size limit.

front: What do S3's '11 nines' of durability mean in practice?
back: S3 provides 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability — statistically, if you store 10 million objects, you'd expect to lose one every 10,000 years. This is achieved by automatically replicating data across ≥3 AZs. Storage is effectively unlimited with no provisioning. Throughput: 5,500 GETs/s and 3,500 PUTs/s per prefix, scalable by distributing across prefixes.

front: Why do CDN edge nodes deliver content in under 50ms globally?
back: CDNs deploy 200+ Points of Presence (PoPs) worldwide, caching content at the network edge closest to users. A request travels to a nearby PoP (~10-30ms) instead of crossing continents to the origin server (~100-300ms). Static assets get cache-hit latencies of 5-20ms. Dynamic content can be accelerated via persistent connections to origin and TCP optimization at the edge.

front: What are the typical latency numbers for DNS lookup, SSD read, and network round trips?
back: DNS lookup: 20-120ms (cached ~0ms). SSD random read: ~100μs (100x faster than HDD's ~10ms). Same-datacenter network round trip: ~0.5ms. Cross-continent round trip: ~100-150ms (limited by speed of light). These numbers matter for system design because they determine where caching, co-location, and batching have the most impact.

front: How do the latency tiers compare: memory, SSD, disk, same-DC network, cross-continent?
back: L1 cache: ~1ns. RAM: ~100ns. SSD random read: ~100μs. HDD random read: ~10ms. Same-datacenter round trip: ~0.5ms. Cross-continent round trip: ~150ms. Each tier is roughly 10-1000x slower than the previous. This is why in-memory caches (Redis) are ~1000x faster than disk-based databases, and why co-locating services in the same region matters.

front: What back-of-envelope numbers should you know for capacity estimation?
back: 1 day = 86,400s ≈ 100K seconds. 1M daily users ≈ ~12 QPS average, ~100 QPS peak. 1 char = 1 byte, 1 int = 4-8 bytes, 1 image ≈ 200KB-2MB. 1TB = 1 billion KB. A single server handles ~10K concurrent connections. Redis: 100K ops/s. Postgres: 10K queries/s. Kafka: 1M msgs/s. These anchors let you estimate whether a design fits the scale.

front: What is the bandwidth capacity of modern networks, and why does it matter for system design?
back: A 1Gbps link transfers ~125MB/s; 10Gbps ≈ 1.25GB/s. Cross-region bandwidth is expensive ($0.01-0.09/GB) and limited. Within a datacenter, bandwidth is cheap and fast. This is why data-intensive processing should be co-located with storage (move compute to data, not data to compute), and why CDNs serve static assets instead of origin servers.

front: What are REST's core principles, and what makes an API truly RESTful?
back: REST uses resources (nouns as URLs), HTTP methods (GET/POST/PUT/DELETE as verbs), and stateless requests (each request carries all needed context). Truly RESTful APIs also use HATEOAS — responses include links to related actions. In practice, most 'REST' APIs are just HTTP JSON APIs using resource URLs and status codes. Strengths: simplicity, cacheability, wide tooling.

front: How does GraphQL solve over-fetching and under-fetching?
back: GraphQL exposes a single endpoint where the client specifies exactly which fields it needs in a query. Over-fetching (getting unused fields) is eliminated because the response shape matches the query. Under-fetching (needing multiple round trips) is solved because related data can be requested in one query via nested fields. Tradeoffs: complex server implementation, N+1 query risk without DataLoader, harder to cache.

front: What is gRPC, and when is it preferred over REST?
back: gRPC uses Protocol Buffers for binary serialization (smaller, faster than JSON) over HTTP/2 (multiplexed streams, header compression). It supports unary, server-streaming, client-streaming, and bidirectional streaming. Preferred for internal microservice communication where performance matters and browser support isn't needed. Codegen from .proto files ensures type-safe client/server contracts.

front: What are the three main API pagination strategies, and when should you use each?
back: Offset-based (LIMIT/OFFSET): simplest, but slow for large offsets and inconsistent if data changes. Cursor-based: encode the last item's position as an opaque cursor; consistent and efficient but no random page access. Keyset (seek): use WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT N; fast and consistent but requires a sortable unique column. Cursor-based is the best default for most APIs.

front: What are the three common API versioning strategies?
back: URL path (/v1/users): most explicit, easy to route, but changes the resource identity. Header (Accept: application/vnd.api+json;version=1): clean URLs, but less discoverable and harder to test in a browser. Query param (/users?version=1): easy to add, but clutters the URL. URL path is most common in practice. Key principle: never break existing clients — add fields, don't remove them.

front: What do rate limiting headers communicate, and how should clients use them?
back: X-RateLimit-Limit: max requests allowed per window. X-RateLimit-Remaining: requests left in current window. X-RateLimit-Reset: Unix timestamp when the window resets. Clients should check Remaining before making requests and back off when close to zero. When rate-limited (HTTP 429), respect Retry-After header. Server-side: use token bucket or sliding window algorithms.

front: What are idempotency keys, and why are they essential for payment APIs?
back: An idempotency key is a unique client-generated ID (usually UUID) sent with a request. The server stores the key and its response; if the same key is sent again, the server returns the cached response instead of re-executing. This makes retries safe — a network timeout on a payment request won't double-charge. Implementation: store key → response in a database with TTL expiry.

front: How do webhooks work, and what reliability challenges do they introduce?
back: Webhooks are HTTP callbacks: when an event occurs, the server sends a POST request to a client-registered URL. This is push-based (no polling), but introduces reliability challenges: the client endpoint may be down, responses may time out, and payloads can be delivered out of order or duplicated. Best practices: sign payloads (HMAC), retry with exponential backoff, include event IDs for deduplication, and provide a replay API.

front: What functions does an API gateway serve, and when is it worth the complexity?
back: An API gateway is a reverse proxy that handles cross-cutting concerns: request routing to microservices, authentication/authorization, rate limiting, request/response transformation, logging, and SSL termination. Worth it when you have multiple backend services and want clients to see one unified API. Examples: Kong, AWS API Gateway, Envoy. Tradeoff: adds latency (1-5ms) and is a single point of failure if not clustered.

front: Long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket: when should you use each?
back: Long polling: client holds an HTTP request open until the server has data, then reconnects — simple, works everywhere, but high overhead per message. SSE (Server-Sent Events): server pushes events over a persistent HTTP connection — unidirectional, auto-reconnects, works through proxies. WebSocket: full-duplex persistent connection — bidirectional, lowest latency, but more complex (no auto-reconnect, proxy issues). Use SSE for notifications/feeds, WebSocket for chat/real-time collaboration, long polling as a fallback.

front: What are the equivalent managed message queue services across AWS, GCP, and Azure?
back: AWS: SQS (simple queue) and SNS (pub/sub fan-out). GCP: Cloud Pub/Sub (unified pub/sub with pull and push subscriptions). Azure: Service Bus (enterprise messaging with queues and topics). SQS is simplest for point-to-point; Pub/Sub is closest to Kafka semantics; Service Bus supports advanced patterns like sessions and dead-lettering natively.

front: What are the equivalent object storage services across AWS, GCP, and Azure?
back: AWS: S3 (the original, 11 nines durability, multiple storage tiers). GCP: Cloud Storage (similar tiers — Standard, Nearline, Coldline, Archive). Azure: Blob Storage (Hot, Cool, Archive tiers). All offer virtually unlimited storage, strong consistency, and lifecycle policies. S3 is the de facto standard; most tools support its API, and some GCP/Azure services offer S3-compatible endpoints.

front: What are the equivalent NoSQL key-value databases across cloud providers?
back: AWS: DynamoDB (fully managed, single-digit ms, partition key + sort key). GCP: Firestore (document-oriented, real-time sync, mobile-friendly) or Bigtable (wide-column, HBase-compatible, analytics scale). Azure: Cosmos DB (multi-model, tunable consistency from strong to eventual, global distribution). DynamoDB is simplest for KV; Cosmos DB is most flexible; Bigtable is for analytical workloads.

front: What are the equivalent managed cache services across cloud providers?
back: AWS: ElastiCache (managed Redis or Memcached). GCP: Memorystore (managed Redis or Memcached). Azure: Azure Cache for Redis. All provide sub-millisecond latency, automatic failover, and cluster mode. Redis is the dominant choice across all clouds due to its data structure support. Key sizing decision: node size (memory) and cluster mode (sharding across nodes for >100GB).

front: What are the equivalent CDN services across cloud providers?
back: AWS: CloudFront (200+ edge locations, integrates with S3/ALB, Lambda@Edge for compute at edge). GCP: Cloud CDN (integrates with Cloud Load Balancing, supports Cache-Control headers). Azure: Azure CDN (multiple provider tiers — Microsoft, Akamai, Verizon). Third-party alternatives: Cloudflare (largest network, free tier, DDoS protection) and Fastly (edge compute via Wasm).

front: What are the equivalent serverless compute services across cloud providers?
back: AWS: Lambda (up to 15min runtime, 10GB memory, container image support). GCP: Cloud Functions (similar, plus Cloud Run for containers with longer runtimes). Azure: Azure Functions (supports Durable Functions for stateful orchestration). All charge per invocation + duration. Cold start latency (100ms-10s) is the main tradeoff. For longer workloads, Cloud Run / AWS Fargate / Azure Container Apps bridge the gap.

front: What are the equivalent container orchestration services across cloud providers?
back: AWS: EKS (managed Kubernetes) or ECS (AWS-native, simpler). GCP: GKE (widely considered the best managed K8s — Google invented Kubernetes). Azure: AKS (managed Kubernetes with strong Azure AD integration). All run the same Kubernetes API, so workloads are portable. GKE has the smoothest experience; ECS is simpler if you're all-in on AWS and don't need K8s portability.

front: What are the main managed search service options?
back: AWS: OpenSearch Service (fork of Elasticsearch, managed). All clouds: self-managed Elasticsearch on VMs/containers. Third-party: Algolia (hosted search-as-a-service, ~100ms, easy to integrate, but expensive at scale). Elasticsearch/OpenSearch uses inverted indexes for full-text search with BM25 ranking. For vector/semantic search, all now support kNN with vector embeddings.

front: What are the equivalent stream processing services across cloud providers?
back: AWS: Kinesis Data Streams (real-time ingestion) + Kinesis Data Analytics (SQL/Flink on streams). GCP: Pub/Sub (ingestion) + Dataflow (Apache Beam runner, unified batch+stream). Azure: Event Hubs (ingestion, Kafka-compatible) + Stream Analytics (SQL on streams). Kafka is the cross-cloud alternative. Kinesis is simplest for AWS-native; Dataflow is most powerful for complex transformations.

front: What are the equivalent managed DNS services across cloud providers?
back: AWS: Route 53 (DNS + health checks + routing policies: latency, geolocation, failover, weighted). GCP: Cloud DNS (fast, 100% SLA, but fewer routing policies). Azure: Azure DNS (integrates with Traffic Manager for advanced routing). Route 53 is the most feature-rich with built-in health-checked failover. All support DNSSEC. Typical propagation: seconds to minutes within the provider, longer for internet-wide TTL expiry.
